people.desc: The eternal Creator of heaven and earth who forms a covenant with Israel, speaks through the prophets, and is revealed throughout Scripture as sovereign over all creation.
Son of Mary, raised by Joseph the carpenter; a Galilean teacher whose ministry, crucifixion, and resurrection form the center of the New Testament.
Son of Isaac and Rebekah, twin brother of Esau, whose name was changed to Israel after wrestling with God; father of the twelve tribal ancestors.
Youngest son of Jesse, a shepherd who killed the giant Goliath and later became Israel's second king, uniting the tribes and making Jerusalem his capital.
Hebrew raised in Pharaoh's household who led Israel out of slavery in Egypt, received the law at Sinai, and guided the nation through the wilderness.
Older brother of Moses who served as his spokesman before Pharaoh and became Israel's first high priest.
Called by God to leave Ur for Canaan, husband of Sarah and father of Isaac, regarded as the ancestor through whom God's covenant promises were given.
Son of David and Bathsheba who succeeded his father as king, known for his wisdom, vast wealth, and building the temple in Jerusalem.
Son of Kish from the tribe of Benjamin, anointed by Samuel as Israel's first king, whose reign ended in disobedience and rejection by God.
The Spirit of God active in creation, empowering judges and prophets in the Old Testament, and poured out on believers at Pentecost in the New Testament.
Fourth son of Jacob and Leah, whose proposal spared Joseph's life; his descendants became the tribe from which David and Jesus descended.
Favored son of Jacob and Rachel, sold into slavery by his brothers, who rose to become governor of Egypt and later saved his family from famine.
Son of Nun who served as Moses' military aide and successor, leading Israel across the Jordan and conquering the land of Canaan.
Former Pharisee named Saul who persecuted the early church until his conversion on the road to Damascus, becoming the leading missionary apostle to the Gentiles.
Galilean fisherman called by Jesus to be one of his twelve apostles, later a prominent leader and preacher in the early Jerusalem church.
Younger son of Joseph, born in Egypt, whose descendants became a leading tribe of Israel after receiving Jacob's blessing over his older brother.
Youngest son of Jacob, born to Rachel who died giving birth to him; his descendants became the tribe that later produced Israel's first king.
Elder twin son of Isaac and Rebekah, a skilled hunter who sold his birthright to his brother Jacob and became ancestor of the Edomites.
Son of Lot, born through his elder daughter after they fled the destruction of Sodom, and ancestor of the Moabite nation east of the Dead Sea.
The unnamed Egyptian king who enslaved the Israelites and resisted Moses' demands for their release until a series of plagues forced him to let them go.
Prophet from Anathoth who warned Judah of coming judgment and the Babylonian exile, enduring persecution while urging surrender rather than resistance.
Son of Abraham and Sarah born in their old age, nearly offered as a sacrifice on Mount Moriah, and father of Esau and Jacob.
Prophet and last of Israel's judges, dedicated to the Lord from birth by his mother Hannah, who anointed both Saul and David as king.
Nephew of David through his sister Zeruiah, commander of David's army known for his military skill and ruthless elimination of rivals.
King of Judah, son of Ahaz, remembered for religious reforms, withstanding the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem, and a miraculous extension of his life.
Elder son of Joseph, born in Egypt, whose tribe received territory on both sides of the Jordan despite being passed over for Jacob's greater blessing.
Prophet from Tishbe who confronted King Ahab and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel and was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind.
Son of David known for his striking appearance, who avenged his sister Tamar's rape and later led an armed rebellion against his father.
Ascetic prophet who preached repentance in the wilderness and baptized Jesus in the Jordan River before being executed by Herod Antipas.
King of Babylon who besieged and destroyed Jerusalem, carried the people of Judah into exile, and, according to Daniel, was later humbled by a period of madness.
Son of Ham cursed by his grandfather Noah, whose descendants settled the land later promised to Abraham's offspring.
Son of King Saul known for his close friendship with David, whose loyalty to David he protected even against his own father's wishes.
Former official under Solomon who led the northern tribes to secede, becoming the first king of Israel and setting up rival worship sites at Bethel and Dan.
King of Israel married to Jezebel, whose promotion of Baal worship brought him into repeated conflict with the prophet Elijah.
Judean noble taken captive to Babylon, known for interpreting the dreams of kings and surviving a night in a den of lions because of his faithfulness.
Firstborn son of Jacob and Leah who lost his birthright after violating his father's concubine, though he later tried to save Joseph from his brothers.
King of Judah, son of Asa, remembered for religious reforms and an alliance with the northern kingdom that drew criticism from the prophets.
Third son of Jacob and Leah, whose descendants became the priestly tribe responsible for Israel's tabernacle and temple worship.
Son of Jacob born to Rachel's servant Bilhah, whose tribe later migrated north and became associated with idolatrous worship.
The Egyptian king who elevated Joseph to power after he interpreted dreams warning of coming famine, placing him second in command over Egypt.
Aaron's son and successor as high priest, he took on leadership of the priesthood after his father's death and was the father of Phinehas.
A non-Israelite seer hired by King Balak of Moab to curse Israel, who instead blessed them under God's constraint and whose donkey famously spoke to rebuke him.
Son of Jacob born to Leah's servant Zilpah, whose descendants became one of the twelve tribes of Israel.
The adversary who accuses Job before God and tests his faith through suffering, and who later tempts Jesus in the wilderness before his ministry begins.
Roman governor of Judea who presided over Jesus' trial, yielded to the crowd's demand for crucifixion despite finding no guilt in him, and ordered the sentence carried out.
Commander of King Saul's army and son of Ner, who backed Saul's son Ish-bosheth as king before being killed by Joab in revenge for a kinsman's death.
King of Judah, son of Abijah and father of Jehoshaphat, remembered for tearing down idols and pagan altars during a long reign of religious reform.
Prophet who succeeded Elijah after receiving a double portion of his spirit, performing miracles such as healing Naaman's leprosy and multiplying a widow's jar of oil.
Son of Amoz and major prophet in Judah during the reigns of several kings, who advised Hezekiah and authored the prophetic book bearing his name.
A wealthy, upright man from the land of Uz whose faith was tested through the sudden loss of his family, health, and possessions, the central figure of the book of Job.
Canaanite storm and fertility god whose worship repeatedly drew Israel into idolatry, most famously confronted by Elijah in the contest on Mount Carmel.
Son of Josiah and the last king of Judah, installed on the throne by Babylon, whose rebellion led to Jerusalem's fall and his own capture and blinding.
Jewish official in the Persian royal court and cousin and guardian of Esther, who exposed a plot against the king and helped thwart Haman's scheme to destroy the Jews.
A judge of Israel who defeated a vast Midianite army with only three hundred men after God pared down his forces, and who later fathered Abimelech.
King of Judah who launched sweeping religious reforms after the Book of the Law was rediscovered in the temple during repairs, and father of Jehoiakim and Zedekiah.
Son of Jacob born to Bilhah, Rachel's servant, whose descendants formed the tribe of Naphtali in northern Israel.
Wife of Abraham who remained childless for decades before bearing Isaac in her old age as God had promised.
King of Israel who violently overthrew the house of Ahab, killing Jezebel and Joram, and worked to purge Baal worship from the northern kingdom.
Righteous man instructed by God to build an ark that preserved his family and pairs of animals through a great flood that covered the earth.
Jewish queen of Persia and cousin of Mordecai, who risked her life to intercede with King Ahasuerus and save her people from Haman's plot to destroy them.
Brother of Rebekah and father of Leah and Rachel, who took in his nephew Jacob as a laborer and repeatedly changed the terms of his wages.
Son of Jacob and Leah whose descendants became the tribe of Zebulun, one of the twelve tribes settled in the land of Israel.
Persian official who plotted the annihilation of the Jews out of hatred for Mordecai, and was ultimately hanged on the gallows he had built for him.
Jacob's favored wife and younger sister of Leah, mother of Joseph and Benjamin, who died giving birth to the latter on the way to Bethlehem.
Father of David from Bethlehem, whose youngest son was anointed king by Samuel after his older sons were passed over.
Son of Jacob born to Leah's servant Zilpah, whose descendants formed the tribe of Asher.
Son and successor of Solomon whose harsh response to the people's grievances triggered the split of the united kingdom into Israel and Judah.
King of Moab who, alarmed by Israel's approach, hired the seer Balaam to pronounce curses against them.
Son of Jacob and Leah who, together with his brother Levi, violently avenged their sister Dinah's rape by slaughtering the men of Shechem.
Priest who remained loyal to David during Absalom's rebellion and later anointed Solomon as king, and was the father of Ahimaaz.
Son of Jacob and Leah whose descendants formed the tribe of Issachar.
Son of Levi and ancestor of one of the three Levitical clans, assigned responsibility for carrying the tabernacle's frames and structural components.
Son of Abraham by his wife Keturah, and ancestor of the Midianite people, who feature repeatedly in Israel's early history.
Judge of Israel given extraordinary strength tied to his Nazirite vow, famed for his exploits against the Philistines and his betrayal by Delilah.
King of Judah and father of Hezekiah, criticized for embracing idolatry and for seeking Assyrian aid against his enemies rather than trusting God.
Son of Josiah placed on Judah's throne by Pharaoh Necho, remembered for defying Jeremiah's warnings and burning the scroll of his prophecies.
Son of Gideon who murdered his seventy brothers to seize power over Shechem, and later died in battle when a woman dropped a millstone on his head.
Son of Zebedee and brother of James, one of Jesus' twelve apostles and part of his inner circle, traditionally credited with the Gospel and Revelation bearing his name.
King of Judah, son of Joash and father of Uzziah, who defeated Edom in battle but then adopted the gods of the people he had conquered.
Abraham's nephew who settled in Sodom and was rescued by angels before its destruction, later becoming father of Moab through his own daughters.
Amorite king who ruled from Heshbon and refused Israel safe passage through his land, leading to his defeat and the conquest of his territory east of the Jordan.
King of Judah, son of Amaziah and father of Jotham, whose long and prosperous reign ended when he was struck with leprosy for presumptuously burning incense in the temple.
Levite musician whom David placed in charge of temple worship and song; several psalms bear his name as author.
Laban's elder daughter, given to Jacob in place of Rachel through her father's deception, and mother of six sons including Judah and Levi.
One of the twelve spies Moses sent into Canaan; alongside Joshua he urged Israel to trust God and take the land, and was rewarded with Hebron as his inheritance.
Priest and judge at Shiloh who raised the boy Samuel; his corrupt sons brought disaster on Israel and the ark of the covenant was captured during his lifetime.
Ephraimite remembered chiefly as the father of Joshua, Moses' successor.
Priest who fled to David after Saul massacred the priests of Nob and served as his priest through his reign, until Solomon removed him for backing Adonijah's bid for the throne.
Persian king, generally identified with Xerxes I, who deposed Queen Vashti and married Esther, whose royal court is the setting for the book of Esther.
Cypriot Levite who sold his land for the early church, introduced the converted Paul to the apostles, and traveled with him as a missionary before their eventual falling out.
Son of Levi and grandfather of Moses and Aaron, whose descendants, the Kohathites, were charged with carrying the ark and other sacred furnishings of the tabernacle.
Prophet in David's court who confronted the king over his adultery with Bathsheba and the killing of Uriah through the parable of the poor man's ewe lamb.
Isaac's wife, chosen at a well by Abraham's servant; mother of Jacob and Esau, she favored Jacob and helped him obtain his father's blessing in Esau's place.
Davidic descendant who led the first wave of exiles back from Babylon to Judah and directed the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem.
The first man, formed by God from the dust and placed in the garden of Eden, whose disobedience brought sin into the world; father of Cain, Abel, and Seth.
King of Judah, son of Jehoram and Athaliah, killed by Jehu while visiting his ally Joram of Israel after only a brief reign.
King of Israel who seized the throne by assassinating Nadab and wiping out the house of Jeroboam, and who warred repeatedly with Judah.
Judean official appointed governor over the land by the Babylonians after Jerusalem's fall, assassinated soon after by Ishmael son of Nethaniah.
High priest who hid the infant king Joash from Athaliah's purge of the royal line and later led the coup that placed him on the throne.
Judge of Israel who defeated the Ammonites but is remembered for the rash vow that led him to sacrifice his own daughter.
Levite who led a rebellion against the leadership of Moses and Aaron in the wilderness and was swallowed up by the earth along with his followers.
Eldest son of Levi and ancestor of the Gershonite clan, who were responsible for transporting the tabernacle's curtains and coverings.
Ephraimite remembered as the father of Jeroboam, who became the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel.
David's sister and mother of his three chief military commanders, Joab, Abishai, and Asahel.
Son of Zeruiah and David's nephew, a fiercely loyal warrior who fought alongside his brother Joab in many of David's battles.
David's son who tried to claim the throne while his father was still alive, was passed over in favor of Solomon, and was later put to death for renewing his ambitions.
Wealthy landowner of Bethlehem who married the widow Ruth as her kinsman-redeemer, becoming an ancestor of David.
Prophet who fled by sea rather than preach to Nineveh, was swallowed by a great fish, and afterward reluctantly delivered God's warning to the city.
King of Judah, son of Hezekiah, whose long reign was marked by idolatry and bloodshed but who repented after being taken captive to Babylon.
Young coworker of Paul, son of a Jewish mother and Greek father, who traveled with him on his missionary journeys and received two New Testament letters bearing his name.
King of Gerar who took Sarah into his household after Abraham presented her as his sister, and later made a covenant with both Abraham and Isaac.
Son of the priest Jehoiada and commander of David's royal bodyguard, noted for his valor, who later helped secure the throne for Solomon and became his army commander.
Tetrarch of Galilee who had John the Baptist beheaded and later questioned Jesus before his crucifixion.
King of Tyre who supplied cedar wood and skilled craftsmen for David's palace and Solomon's temple.
King of Israel, son of Jehoahaz, who visited the dying prophet Elisha for a final word of victory and defeated Amaziah of Judah in battle.
One of the twelve disciples who betrayed Jesus to the chief priests for thirty pieces of silver.
Royal scribe under King Josiah who read aloud the newly discovered Book of the Law, prompting the king's reforms.
Grandson of Esau and ancestor of the Amalekites, a people who attacked Israel in the wilderness and remained a persistent enemy for generations.
Priest and scribe who led a group of exiles back to Jerusalem from Babylon, taught the Law to the people, and worked to end intermarriage with surrounding nations.
King of Bashan, described as a giant, whose kingdom was conquered by Israel alongside Sihon's during the journey toward the Promised Land.
A Hittite soldier in David's army and the husband of Bathsheba; David arranged his death in battle to cover up his affair with her.
David's eldest son, who raped his half-sister Tamar and was later killed by her full brother Absalom in revenge.
Scribe and close aide to the prophet Jeremiah, who wrote down and publicly read Jeremiah's prophecies from dictation.
An Aramean official anointed by Elijah as future king of Aram, who murdered his master Ben-hadad and later warred repeatedly against Israel and Judah.
Son of Nethaniah and a member of the royal line of Judah who assassinated Gedaliah, the Babylonian-appointed governor, after Jerusalem's fall.
A king of Judah who reigned only a few months before being deported to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar; later released from prison and given honor at the Babylonian court.
Father of Benaiah, one of David's chief warriors who commanded the king's bodyguard of Cherethites and Pelethites.
High priest who returned from Babylonian exile alongside Zerubbabel and helped lead the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple.
The mother of Jesus, a young woman of Nazareth betrothed to Joseph who bore Jesus and later appears among his followers after his ascension.
King of Judah, son of Rehoboam and father of Asa, who ruled briefly and fought a war against Jeroboam of the northern kingdom.
Philistine king of Gath who sheltered David when he fled from Saul, later giving him the town of Ziklag.
Court official under King Josiah, son of Shaphan and father of Gedaliah, who protected the prophet Jeremiah from execution.
High priest during King Josiah's reign who discovered the Book of the Law in the temple, sparking Josiah's religious reforms.
Youngest son of Aaron and a priest, from whom a line of priests descended that included Eli.
Phoenician-born wife of King Ahab of Israel who promoted Baal worship, persecuted the prophets, and engineered Naboth's death for his vineyard.
King of Judah, son of Uzziah and father of Ahaz, remembered for strengthening Judah's defenses and building projects.
A widow of Bethlehem who moved to Moab and back, and whose Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth stayed loyally by her side.
Persian king who conquered Babylon and issued the decree allowing exiled Jews to return home and rebuild the Jerusalem temple.
King of Judah who was hidden as an infant from Athaliah's massacre, crowned at age seven, and directed repairs to the temple.
Son of Ahab and Jezebel who became king of Israel and was killed by Jehu during a violent purge of Ahab's dynasty.
Name borne by a succession of Aramean kings of Damascus who repeatedly clashed with and made treaties against Israel and Judah.
King of Zobah in Aram whose forces David defeated, and who later allied with the Ammonites against Israel.
Son of Abraham and Hagar, born before Isaac, whose descendants became the Ishmaelite peoples of the wilderness.
Son of Zebedee and brother of John, one of the twelve apostles and part of Jesus' inner circle, later executed by Herod Agrippa I.
One of Daniel's three Judean companions in Babylon, given a new name, who was thrown into a fiery furnace for refusing to worship an idol and emerged unharmed.
A prophet who accurately foretold King Ahab's death in battle despite the false assurances of Ahab's other prophets, and was imprisoned for it.
A wealthy but harsh sheep owner in Carmel who refused hospitality to David's men; he died soon after, and his widow Abigail became David's wife.
A Jezreelite who owned a vineyard coveted by King Ahab; he was falsely accused and stoned to death at Jezebel's instigation so Ahab could seize the land.
One of Daniel's three Judean companions in Babylon, given a new name, who survived being cast into a fiery furnace for refusing to bow to an idol.
A trusted royal counselor of David who defected to Absalom's rebellion and hanged himself after his strategic advice was rejected.
Son of Manasseh and ancestor of a clan of warriors that settled the region of Gilead east of the Jordan.
A man from the hill country of Ephraim who made a household idol and hired a Levite as his personal priest, whose shrine was later seized by the tribe of Dan.
A Jebusite landowner, also called Araunah, whose threshing floor David purchased as the site for an altar, later the location of Solomon's temple.
One of Noah's three sons who survived the flood, blessed by his father and regarded as ancestor of the Semitic peoples.
A leading figure in the early Jerusalem church who became Paul's traveling companion, was imprisoned with him in Philippi, and later assisted Peter.
Commander of the Canaanite army defeated by Deborah and Barak, who was killed by Jael after fleeing to her tent for refuge.
The firstborn son of Adam and Eve, a farmer who murdered his brother Abel out of jealousy and was banished to wander as a result.
A Persian king during whose reign the decree to rebuild the Jerusalem temple was reaffirmed and the temple work was finally completed.
King of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat and husband of Athaliah, who killed his brothers upon taking the throne and led Judah into idolatry.
Priest of Midian and father-in-law of Moses, who sheltered Moses in exile and later advised him to delegate judicial duties to other leaders.
Daughter of Saul and sister of Jonathan, Michal became David's wife, helped him escape her father's assassins, and later despised him for dancing before the ark.
Father of Ishmael, the man who assassinated Gedaliah, the Babylonian-appointed governor of Judah, after the fall of Jerusalem.
One of the seven men chosen to oversee food distribution in the early Jerusalem church; he later preached in Samaria and baptized the Ethiopian eunuch.
Grandson of Aaron and son of Eleazar, he halted a plague among Israel by killing an Israelite man and a Midianite woman for their idolatry at Baal-Peor.
An Assyrian military officer sent by Sennacherib to demand Jerusalem's surrender, delivering a taunting speech against Hezekiah and the God of Israel.
King of Judah who succeeded his father Manasseh and continued his idolatrous practices; he was assassinated by his own servants after a short reign.
Daughter of Ahab and Jezebel who married into Judah's royal line; after her son Ahaziah's death she seized the throne and killed the rest of the royal family.
A brother of Jesus who did not believe in him during his ministry but became a leading figure in the Jerusalem church, traditionally credited with writing the epistle bearing his name.
Father of Caleb, one of the twelve spies sent into Canaan and later a leader of the tribe of Judah.
Son of Kareah and an army commander who warned Gedaliah of a plot against him; after Gedaliah's murder he led surviving Judeans, including Jeremiah, into Egypt.
A carpenter of Nazareth betrothed to Mary; he raised Jesus as his legal father and, warned in dreams, fled with his family to Egypt to escape Herod.
Captain of Nebuchadnezzar's royal guard who oversaw the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple and the deportation of its people to Babylon.
Son of Judah by Tamar, twin brother of Zerah, born in an unusual birth involving a scarlet thread; an ancestor of Boaz and David.
One of the twelve apostles, from Bethsaida, who brought Nathanael to Jesus and later asked at the Last Supper to be shown the Father.
Son of the Hivite prince Hamor; his violation of Jacob's daughter Dinah led Simeon and Levi to kill him and the men of his city.
A relative of Saul who cursed and threw stones at David during Absalom's rebellion; later spared by David but ultimately executed under Solomon.
Wise wife of the wealthy but foolish Nabal; she interceded with gifts to stop David from taking revenge and, after Nabal's death, became David's wife.
A swift-footed nephew of David, brother of Joab and Abishai, who was killed by Abner while pursuing him in battle.
One of Noah's three sons who survived the flood; his exposure of his father's drunken nakedness led Noah to pronounce a curse on Ham's son Canaan.
Son of Jehu who reigned as king of Israel; Scripture records his kingdom oppressed by Aram until he sought the Lord's help.
King of Israel, son of Joash, who restored the nation's borders during a long, militarily successful reign that the prophet Amos condemned as spiritually corrupt.
Father of Johanan, one of the Judean army commanders active in the land after the fall of Jerusalem.
A Danite from Zorah whose barren wife was visited by the angel of the Lord announcing the birth of their son Samson.
A woman from Magdala whom Jesus freed from seven demons; she followed and supported his ministry and was the first to see him after his resurrection.
Crippled in both feet after a childhood accident, this son of Jonathan was shown kindness by David, who restored his grandfather Saul's land and gave him a place at the royal table.
Father of Abner and uncle of King Saul, belonging to the tribe of Benjamin.
King of Assyria who invaded Judah and besieged Jerusalem during Hezekiah's reign; his army was struck down and he was later assassinated by his own sons.
Son of the priest Zadok who served as a messenger for David, notably outrunning another courier to bring news of Absalom's death.
Father of the prophet Isaiah, otherwise unmentioned in Scripture apart from this relationship.
Commanded by Deborah to lead Israel's army against the Canaanite general Sisera; he insisted Deborah accompany him and is later listed among the faithful in Hebrews.
A prophet who served as David's seer, delivering messages from God including the choice of punishment offered after David's census.
Hivite ruler of Shechem whose son's assault on Dinah led to his and his city's men being killed by Jacob's sons Simeon and Levi.
Son of Pharez and grandson of Judah, listed among the ancestors of David in the genealogies of Ruth and Matthew.
David's loyal friend the Archite, who feigned allegiance to Absalom in order to counter Ahithophel's counsel and warn David of the rebellion's plans.
A Levite chief musician under David, also called Ethan, whose descendants were appointed to prophesy with instruments in temple worship.
A Benjamite and the father of King Saul; while searching for his father's lost donkeys, Saul was anointed Israel's first king.
King of Israel who founded the city of Samaria as his capital and established a dynasty, later condemned by the prophet Micah for his wicked statutes.
Father of Pekah, who conspired against and succeeded King Pekahiah to become king of Israel.
A Moabite widow who left her homeland to stay with her mother-in-law Naomi, gleaned in Boaz's fields, and became his wife and an ancestor of David.
A daughter of David who was raped by her half-brother Amnon, an act her full brother Absalom later avenged by killing Amnon.

places.desc: Capital of the united kingdom under David and Solomon and later of Judah, home to Solomon's Temple, and the city where Jesus was crucified and rose again.
Land where Abraham and later Joseph's family sojourned, where the Israelites were enslaved for generations, and from which Moses led them out in the Exodus.
Originally the Jebusite fortress hill David captured to found his city, the name came to stand for Jerusalem and its Temple as the place of God's dwelling.
The river Israel crossed on dry ground into the Promised Land under Joshua, and centuries later the site where John the Baptist baptized Jesus.
Capital of the Neo-Babylonian empire under Nebuchadnezzar, whose armies destroyed Solomon's Temple and carried Judah into exile in the sixth century BC.
Kingdom east of the Dead Sea descended from Lot, a recurring adversary of Israel, and the homeland Ruth left to follow Naomi to Bethlehem.
Capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, built by King Omri and expanded by Ahab, later giving its name to the Samaritan people of Jesus's day.
The land promised to Abraham's descendants and inhabited by various peoples before Israel entered and settled it under Joshua's leadership.
Dominant Mesopotamian empire that conquered the northern kingdom of Israel and deported its population in 722 BC.
Kingdom south of the Dead Sea descended from Esau, often locked in conflict with Israel and Judah and condemned by several prophets.
Mountainous region east of the Jordan settled by Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, known for its healing balm and as Jephthah's homeland.
Mountain range north of Israel famed for its towering cedar trees, which Solomon imported to build the Temple and his palace.
Northern hill country around the Sea of Galilee where Jesus was raised in Nazareth and carried out most of his public ministry.
Fortified city near the Jordan whose walls collapsed after Joshua's army marched around it seven times, the first Canaanite city Israel conquered.
Town north of Jerusalem where Jacob dreamed of a stairway to heaven; later became a rival royal sanctuary set up by Jeroboam.
Roman-era name for the hill country of southern Israel, the setting for much of the Gospel narratives and Jesus's Judean ministry.
Fertile plateau east of the Jordan and north of Gilead, ruled by King Og until Israel defeated him, and known for its cattle and oaks.
Aramean kingdom northeast of Israel centered on Damascus, a frequent military rival of Israel and Judah through the era of the kings.
Capital of the Aramean kingdom of Syria and the city near which Saul, later Paul, was confronted by the risen Christ on the road.
Phoenician port city whose king Hiram supplied cedar and craftsmen for David and Solomon's building projects, later denounced by prophets for its pride.
Great Mesopotamian river marking one boundary of the land promised to Abraham and the region where Babylon and Assyria arose.
Arid southern region of Canaan traversed by the patriarchs and scouted by the twelve spies Moses sent from Kadesh.
Ancient city where Abraham purchased the cave of Machpelah to bury Sarah and where David first reigned as king over Judah.
City of the plain, associated with Gomorrah, destroyed by fire and sulfur for its wickedness in the days of Abraham and his nephew Lot.
Southern border town linked to wells dug by Abraham and Isaac, often paired with Dan in the phrase describing the full extent of Israel's land.
Phoenician coastal city north of Tyre, an ancestral Canaanite city that Jesus and his disciples briefly visited during his ministry.
One of the five principal Philistine cities and the hometown of the giant warrior Goliath, whom David slew.
Canaanite city whose people tricked Joshua into a treaty through deception, later the site of a battle where the sun stood still at Joshua's command.
Small Galilean village where Jesus grew up with Mary and Joseph, giving him the identifying title "Jesus of Nazareth."
Camp near Jericho where Israel first stayed after crossing the Jordan, where the men were circumcised and the Passover kept in the new land.
Region east of the Gulf of Aqaba settled by descendants of Abraham through Keturah, where Moses fled Egypt and married Zipporah.
Body of water God parted before the fleeing Israelites, whose waters then closed over the pursuing Egyptian army under Moses.
Town in Judah, birthplace of King David and the setting of the book of Ruth, later where the prophets said Israel's ruler would be born and where Jesus was born.
Town in Benjamin that became King Saul's hometown and capital, earlier notorious as the site of a brutal crime in Judges that provoked civil war.
Syrian city on the Orontes River repeatedly cited in Scripture as marking the northern limit of Israel's territory.
City between Mount Ebal and Gerizim where Abraham first built an altar in Canaan and where Joshua later led Israel in renewing the covenant.
Coastal mountain range where the prophet Elijah confronted and defeated the prophets of Baal in a contest to call down fire.
Capital city of the Amorite king Sihon, conquered by Israel as they journeyed toward the Jordan before entering Canaan.
Hill in Jerusalem holding the Temple, celebrated throughout the Psalms and the Prophets as the symbolic dwelling place of God among his people.
Southernmost of the five Philistine cities, where the blinded Samson was imprisoned and died pulling down the temple of Dagon.
City of the plain destroyed together with Sodom for its wickedness, and afterward invoked repeatedly as a byword for divine judgment.
Northernmost town of Israel, named for the tribe that migrated there and set up an idolatrous shrine that led the region astray.
Egypt's great river where the infant Moses was hidden among the reeds and which turned to blood in the first of the plagues.
Town in Ephraim that housed the tabernacle and the ark of the covenant before the Temple was built, where the boy Samuel ministered before Eli.
Rift valley running from the Sea of Galilee down through the Dead Sea toward the Gulf of Aqaba, used to describe Israel's eastern border.
Region south of Egypt, roughly Nubia, listed among the descendants of Noah and elsewhere depicted as a distant and formidable people.
Roman province in northern Greece where Paul received his vision of a man pleading "come over and help us," leading him to found churches at Philippi and Thessalonica.
Mountainous territory that became the homeland of Edom, settled by the descendants of Esau.
Priestly town near Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin, the hometown of the prophet Jeremiah.
Levitical town in Benjamin near the Philistine frontier, the staging point for Jonathan's daring raid on a Philistine garrison.

A distant western seaport, likely in the far Mediterranean, famed for its trading ships; Jonah booked passage there to flee from God, and Solomon's fleet returned from it laden with gold, silver, and exotic goods.
A Roman province occupying western Asia Minor, with Ephesus as its capital; a major field of Paul's missionary work and home to the seven churches addressed in Revelation.
A heavily fortified city in the Judean lowlands, second in importance to Jerusalem, conquered by Joshua and later besieged and famously depicted in relief by the Assyrian king Sennacherib.
The empire that overthrew Babylon under Cyrus the Great and permitted the exiled Jews to return home; its kings and court dominate the narratives of Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, and Daniel.
A town in Benjamin's territory near Gibeah, fortified by King Baasha of Israel to block travel to Judah until Asa had it dismantled; also near the site where Deborah held court.
A fishing village on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee that served as the base of Jesus' Galilean ministry, home to Peter, and the setting for numerous healings and teachings.

The northernmost of the five Philistine city-states, associated with the worship of Baal-zebub and one of the cities the captured ark of the covenant passed through before its plagues drove the Philistines to return it.
A name used for the mountain of God in the Sinai wilderness, the site of the burning bush where God called Moses and, later, of Elijah's encounter with the still small voice.
The mountain in the wilderness where God appeared to Moses in fire and smoke and gave Israel the Ten Commandments and the covenant law after the exodus from Egypt.
One of the five Philistine city-states, site of the temple where the captured ark of the covenant was set beside the idol Dagon, which fell and broke before it.
A Canaanite royal city taken by Joshua, later a Levitical city in Judah that revolted from King Jehoram's rule and was besieged by Sennacherib's Assyrian army.
The capital of the Assyrian Empire on the Tigris River, sent the reluctant prophet Jonah to warn of its destruction, and later condemned by Nahum for its cruelty and idolatry.
The wilderness peninsula through which Israel journeyed after leaving Egypt, encompassing the mountain where the law was given and where the people camped for roughly a year.

A major port city in the Roman province of Asia where Paul ministered for over two years, sparking a riot among silversmiths devoted to Artemis, and later recipient of his epistle and the first of Revelation's seven letters.
A fortified Canaanite city on Ephraim's border that Pharaoh captured and gave as a wedding dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife, prompting Solomon to rebuild it alongside Hazor and Megiddo.
A town and fertile valley in Issachar's territory, home to Ahab's palace and Naboth's vineyard, and the scene of Jehu's bloody purge of Ahab's dynasty and Jezebel's death.
A northern landmark near the entrance to the territory of Hamath in Syria, repeatedly named as marking the northern extent of the Promised Land and of Solomon's kingdom.
A strategic fortress guarding a key pass into the Jezreel Valley, the scene of numerous battles including King Josiah's death, and the namesake of Armageddon in Revelation.
A ridge east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley where David fled during Absalom's revolt, Jesus taught and wept over the city, prayed the night before his arrest, and ascended into heaven.
The capital city of the Ammonites, besieged by Joab's forces during David's reign and the place where David arranged for Uriah the Hittite to die in battle.
One of the five Philistine city-states on the Mediterranean coast, singled out in prophetic oracles of judgment pronounced against the Philistine cities.
An oasis in the wilderness south of Canaan where Israel camped for much of its wandering; the spies were sent out from there, Miriam died there, and Moses struck the rock in anger.
The town where the ark of the covenant rested for about twenty years after the Philistines returned it, before David finally brought it up to Jerusalem.
A town in Benjamin where Israel gathered for national assemblies and Samuel judged the people, later made the administrative seat of Gedaliah after Jerusalem fell to Babylon.
The innermost chamber of the tabernacle and later the temple, housing the ark of the covenant and entered only once a year by the high priest on the Day of Atonement.
A distant, gold-rich land reached by sea, the source of the fine gold and precious cargo brought back by Solomon's trading fleet.
The hill-country hometown of the prophet Samuel, where he was born, built an altar, judged Israel, and was ultimately buried.
In many passages simply "the River" denotes the Euphrates, used repeatedly to mark the eastern boundary of the land promised to Abraham's descendants.
The low, fertile hill country between the Judean highlands and the Philistine coastal plain, a productive agricultural belt and frequent battleground between Israel and its neighbors.
A Canaanite city near Bethel where Abram once pitched his tent and built an altar, and which Joshua's forces destroyed after an initial defeat brought on by Achan's hidden sin.
A valley and town in Dan's territory where Joshua commanded the sun to stand still while Israel pursued the fleeing Amorite kings.
A kingdom east of the Jordan descended from Lot, a recurring adversary of Israel whose capital was Rabbah and whose downfall was announced by several prophets.
A Roman administrative capital on the Mediterranean coast built by Herod the Great, home to the centurion Cornelius and the site where Paul was held prisoner before sailing to Rome.
A large Mediterranean island, the homeland of Barnabas, and the first stop on Paul and Barnabas's inaugural missionary journey, where they confronted the sorcerer Elymas.
A city in upper Mesopotamia where Abraham's family settled after leaving Ur, and where Jacob later took refuge with his uncle Laban and married Leah and Rachel.
A site in the Negev where Israel first suffered defeat after refusing to enter Canaan, later captured and devoted to destruction by Judah and Simeon.
An Amorite city east of the Jordan captured by Israel, allotted to the tribe of Gad, and later designated a city for the Levites.
A place east of the Jordan where Jacob met angels of God on his way home, later Ish-bosheth's short-lived capital and David's refuge during Absalom's rebellion.
A wealthy kingdom in southern Arabia known for spices, gold, and precious stones, whose queen journeyed to Jerusalem to test Solomon's wisdom.
The Persian Empire's winter capital, the setting of the book of Esther and the place where Nehemiah served as cupbearer to King Artaxerxes.
A Philistine border town given to David by King Achish of Gath during his years as a fugitive from Saul, later raided and burned by Amalekite marauders.
A Roman province covering southern Greece, including Corinth, where Paul spent extended time preaching and to whose churches he later addressed collections and greetings.
A town in the Judean foothills near a cave where David gathered his band of followers and family while fleeing from Saul.
A nomadic people descended from Esau's line who repeatedly attacked Israel, from the wilderness ambush at Rephidim through the campaigns of Saul and David against them.
A town on the rim of the Arnon Gorge east of the Jordan, marking the southern boundary of the territory taken from the Amorites and settled by Reuben.
A village near Jerusalem on the slope of the Mount of Olives, home to Mary, Martha, and Lazarus, where Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead and stayed in his final days.
A border town of Judah where the Philistines sent the captured ark of the covenant back on a cart, and where some of the townspeople were struck down for looking inside it.
A wadi marking the southwestern border between Canaan and Egypt, cited repeatedly as a boundary point in descriptions of the land's territorial extent.
An ancient kingdom east of Mesopotamia whose king Chedorlaomer led a coalition of rulers against Sodom and its neighbors in the time of Abraham; later the subject of prophetic judgment oracles.
The outer chamber of the tabernacle and temple, containing the lampstand, the table of showbread, and the altar of incense, entered daily by the officiating priests.
Oasis in the wilderness of Zin that served as Israel's base camp for decades and the launch point for the twelve spies sent into Canaan.
Nomadic Arab tribe and desert region descended from Ishmael's son Kedar, known in poetic and prophetic texts for its dark tents, flocks, and archers.
Earlier name of Hebron, linked to the Anakim giants; Sarah died there and Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah nearby as a burial site.
Coastal plain southwest of Judah controlled by the Philistines and their five-city league, a persistent military rival of Israel from the judges through the monarchy.

places.n: Valley of the Son of Hinnom
places.desc: Ravine bordering Jerusalem where kings Ahaz and Manasseh practiced child sacrifice to Molech, later defiled by Josiah and used by prophets as an image of coming judgment.
Syrian capital where believers were first called Christians and Paul and Barnabas were commissioned as missionaries, serving as the base for Paul's journeys.
Desert region south and east of Israel inhabited by various tribal peoples; Paul withdrew there for a time after his conversion.
Town belonging to the Gibeonite confederation that tricked Joshua into a treaty; later counted among Benjamin's territory.
Site near Bethel in Benjamin whose name, meaning 'house of wickedness,' prophets applied mockingly to Bethel because of its idol worship.
Fishing village on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, home to Peter, Andrew, and Philip, where Jesus fed a crowd and healed a blind man, yet later denounced for unbelief.
Persian administrative name for the province west of the Euphrates that included Judah, used repeatedly in official correspondence during the rebuilding of Jerusalem.
Roman province in southeastern Asia Minor centered on Tarsus, Paul's home region and an early stop in the spread of the gospel to Gentiles.
Canaanite royal city in Judah's hill country, also called Kiriath-sepher, captured by Joshua and later taken by Othniel.
Small Aramean kingdom northeast of the Sea of Galilee; David married a princess from there, and Absalom fled to it after murdering Amnon.
Hebrew designation for the Mediterranean, marking the western boundary of the land promised to Israel.
Dominant Canaanite city in upper Galilee described as head of the northern kingdoms, burned by Joshua and later rebuilt as a fortress city by Solomon.
Snow-capped peak marking the northern edge of Israelite territory near Bashan, celebrated in the Psalms for its dew and grandeur.
Site in Amorite territory where Israel under Moses defeated King Sihon, opening the way to settle the Transjordan.
Fertile valley and royal town in northern Israel where Ahab and Jezebel had a palace, Naboth's vineyard stood, and Jehu carried out his bloody purge of Ahab's dynasty.
Mediterranean port town from which Jonah tried to flee by ship, and where Peter raised Tabitha and received his vision opening the gospel to Gentiles.
Fortified city of refuge in Naphtali and the home of the judge Barak, later captured by Assyria.
Valley and seasonal streambed east of Jerusalem separating the city from the Mount of Olives, crossed by David fleeing Absalom and by Jesus on the night of his arrest.
Wilderness region in the Sinai peninsula where Israel camped during the exodus and where Ishmael later settled and grew to manhood.
Mountain ridge in Moab, part of the Abarim range, from whose summit Moses viewed the Promised Land shortly before his death.
Capital of the empire that ruled Judea in the New Testament era, the destination of Paul's final voyage and imprisonment and recipient of his letter to the Romans.
Hebrew name for the Dead Sea, forming part of the eastern and southern border of Israelite territory.
Ancient name for the plain of Babylonia in southern Mesopotamia, the setting for the tower of Babel narrative.
Canaanite city near Megiddo in the Jezreel valley allotted to Manasseh, remembered in the Song of Deborah as the site of Barak's battle against Sisera.
Judean hill town south of Bethlehem, home of the prophet Amos and of a wise woman Joab enlisted to intercede for Absalom.
Lowland southwest of Jerusalem where David twice defeated the Philistines after becoming king over all Israel.
Wilderness area that included Kadesh, where Miriam died and Moses struck the rock in disobedience rather than speaking to it.
Aramean kingdom in Syria whose forces Saul and later David fought and subdued, extending Israel's influence northward.
Town on the border of Judah and Dan, home of Samson's father Manoah and the site of Samson's birth and eventual burial.
Town on the Arnon River gorge marking the southern edge of territory taken from the Amorites and assigned to Reuben and Gad.
Syrian city-state near Aleppo conquered by Assyria, cited by Assyrian envoys as proof that no god could withstand their king.
Fortified Judean town in the Shephelah near the valley where David fought Goliath, and one of the last cities holding out against Babylon before Jerusalem's fall.
Mesopotamian empire and region to which Judah's population was exiled under Nebuchadnezzar and from which exiles later returned under Cyrus's decree.
Village near Jerusalem where Shimei cursed David during his flight from Absalom and where Michal's grieving second husband was made to leave her.
Twin towns, Upper and Lower, on the ridge route from Gibeon to the coastal plain, site of Joshua's rout of the Amorite kings when the sun stood still.
Chief city of Edom singled out repeatedly by the prophets as the target of judgment oracles against that nation.
Region of southern Mesopotamia and homeland of the Babylonians, associated with Abraham's origin in Ur and later with Babylon's empire.
North African city whose native Simon was compelled to carry Jesus's cross, and whose Jewish community produced early converts active in the Antioch church.
City of Bashan where Israel under Moses defeated King Og, the last of the giant-descended Rephaim kings.
Oasis and spring on the western shore of the Dead Sea where David hid from Saul in nearby caves and later spared the king's life.
Port on the Gulf of Aqaba used by Solomon's fleet for trade voyages to Ophir and later by Jehoshaphat for a failed shipping venture.
Roman province in central Asia Minor evangelized by Paul on his missionary journeys and later addressed in his letter to the Galatians.
Fertile district in the eastern Nile delta granted to Jacob's family by Joseph, where the Israelites multiplied and were spared several of the plagues.
Stream east of the Jordan where Jacob wrestled through the night with a divine figure before his reunion with Esau, and which later marked a tribal boundary in Gilead.
Town in Gilead that Saul rescued from an Ammonite siege at the start of his reign, and whose men later recovered Saul's body from the wall of Beth-shan.
Original Canaanite name for Bethel, the site where Jacob dreamed of a stairway reaching to heaven and renamed the place.
